title: The salt bridge, and when a cell runs down

screens.h: Why a cell needs a salt bridge
p: Without a salt bridge the voltmeter reads zero. As soon as zinc atoms become Zn²⁺ ions, the zinc half-cell would build up positive charge, and as Cu²⁺ ions are removed, the copper half-cell would be left with extra negative ions.
That charge build-up would stop the flow of electrons almost at once. The salt bridge lets ions move in to cancel it.
**Functions of the salt bridge:** completing the circuit; maintaining electrical neutrality in the half-cells.

screens.h: How it keeps the half-cells neutral
p: The salt bridge is a tube of an electrolyte (for example KNO₃ in agar gel).
At the same time some ions from the half-cells move into the bridge: cations always drift towards the cathode, anions towards the anode.

rules: **Anions (NO₃⁻) move into the ANODE half-cell**, where Zn²⁺ ions are forming.
**Cations (K⁺) move into the CATHODE half-cell**, where Cu²⁺ ions are being used up.

screens.q: A zinc–copper cell has a KNO₃ salt bridge. Which statement is correct while the cell delivers current?
choices: NO₃⁻ ions move into the copper half-cell.
NO₃⁻ moves to the zinc half-cell: anions move into the anode half-cell.
Electrons flow through the salt bridge from Zn to Cu.
Electrons never pass through the bridge.
K⁺ ions move into the copper half-cell.
K⁺ (a cation) moves into the cathode half-cell: the copper half-cell.
The mass of the copper electrode decreases.
Copper is deposited, so its mass increases.
screens.why: C. Anions → anode half-cell; cations → cathode half-cell; electrons only in the wire.

screens.h: Describe how the salt bridge maintains neutrality
p: Name the ions and the half-cells. “Ions flow through the salt bridge” earns nothing on its own.
rules: Say what builds up: “In the anode half-cell Zn²⁺ ions form, so positive charge builds up.”
Ions move both ways: “NO₃⁻ ions move from the salt bridge into the zinc half-cell, and Zn²⁺ ions move from the zinc half-cell into the salt bridge.”
If the cathode is asked too: “In the copper half-cell Cu²⁺ ions are removed, so K⁺ ions move from the salt bridge into it, and anions move from it into the bridge.”

screens.h: Worked example 28.3: the salt bridge in a silver cell
screens.q: A copper half-cell is joined to a silver half-cell by a salt bridge containing KNO₃(aq). (a) State the TWO functions of the salt bridge. (b) Towards which half-cell do the K⁺ ions move? Explain. (c) Explain why a KCℓ salt bridge would be unsuitable.

lines.x: It completes the circuit ✓ and maintains electrical neutrality in the half-cells ✓.

ask.prompt: Towards which half-cell do the K⁺ ions move?
choices: the silver half-cell
Silver is the cathode: K⁺ (a cation) moves into the cathode half-cell.
the copper half-cell
Copper is the anode here: Cu is a stronger reducing agent than Ag. Cations move into the cathode half-cell.

lines.x: Silver is the cathode: Ag⁺ ions are removed from the solution, so K⁺ ions move in to keep the half-cell neutral ✓.
Cℓ⁻ ions from the bridge would react with Ag⁺ ions ✓ to form an AgCℓ precipitate, removing Ag⁺ from the cathode half-cell ✓.

ask.prompt: Why would a KCℓ salt bridge be unsuitable here?
choices: Cℓ⁻ ions would react with Ag⁺ ions and form an AgCℓ precipitate.
That removes Ag⁺ from the cathode half-cell.
KCℓ does not conduct.
KCℓ(aq) conducts: it has free ions. The problem is that Cℓ⁻ reacts with Ag⁺.
K⁺ ions would be reduced at the cathode.
K⁺ is a very weak oxidising agent: it is not reduced. The problem is Cℓ⁻ meeting Ag⁺.

screens.q: Three learners explain why a galvanic cell stops working when the salt bridge is removed.
choices: Thabo: The salt bridge carries the electrons back from the copper half-cell to the zinc half-cell, so without it the electrons are stuck.
Electrons never flow through the bridge, only ions do.
Aisha: Without the bridge, charge builds up in the half-cells and the circuit is open, so no current can flow.
The salt bridge completes the circuit and keeps the half-cells neutral.
Lerato: The salt bridge is where the energy of the cell comes from.
The energy comes from the spontaneous redox reaction.
screens.why: Aisha ✓. The salt bridge completes the circuit and keeps the half-cells neutral. Electrons never flow through the bridge, only ions do.

p: As a cell delivers current, the reactants are used up and the products build up, so the voltage drops, until the cell is “flat”.
The galvanic cell has the capacity to deliver current until the reaction reaches chemical equilibrium or has run to completion. Then the voltage of the cell equals zero.
Think of the cell reaction as an equilibrium: Zn(s) + Cu²⁺(aq) ⇌ Zn²⁺(aq) + Cu(s). More reactant (Cu²⁺) or less product (Zn²⁺): the voltage increases.

rules: **As the cell runs**, [Cu²⁺] falls and [Zn²⁺] rises, so the voltage falls.
**At equilibrium** there is no net reaction: the voltage is **zero**.

screens.h: Worked example 28.9: changing concentrations in a zinc–copper cell
screens.q: A standard zinc–copper cell delivers a current. Predict and explain the effect on the voltage of: (a) replacing the Cu²⁺ solution with a 2 mol·dm⁻³ solution; (b) adding a few drops of concentrated Zn(NO₃)₂ solution to the zinc half-cell; (c) leaving the cell connected for several days.

lines.x: [Cu²⁺], a reactant, increases ✓, so the forward reaction is favoured ✓: the voltage increases ✓.

ask.prompt: (a) The Cu²⁺ solution is made 2 mol·dm⁻³. The voltage…
choices: increases
[Cu²⁺], a reactant, increases, so the forward reaction is favoured.
decreases
Cu²⁺ is a reactant: more reactant favours the forward reaction.
stays the same
Concentration changes the voltage: more reactant favours the forward reaction.

lines.x: [Zn²⁺], a product, increases ✓, so the reverse reaction is favoured ✓: the voltage decreases ✓.

ask.prompt: (b) Concentrated Zn(NO₃)₂ is added to the zinc half-cell. The voltage…
choices: increases
Zn²⁺ is a product: more product favours the reverse reaction.
decreases
[Zn²⁺], a product, increases, so the reverse reaction is favoured.
stays the same
Zn²⁺ is a product of the cell reaction: more product favours the reverse reaction.

lines.x: The reaction approaches equilibrium (or the zinc or Cu²⁺ is used up) ✓, so the voltage decreases to zero ✓.

screens.note: (a) gives a non-standard cell: SAGS reminds you that cell potentials differ when conditions are not standard.

p: **Internal resistance:** opposition to the flow of charge through the electrodes and electrolytes in a cell.
Concentration, gas pressure and temperature change the **emf**. Surface area and the salt bridge change only the **maximum current**.
rules: **Larger electrode surface area:** emf no change; maximum current increases (lower internal resistance; faster reaction).
**Shorter or wider salt bridge:** emf no change; maximum current increases (lower internal resistance).
**More conductive (more concentrated) salt bridge:** emf no change; maximum current increases (lower internal resistance).

screens.q: The emf of a standard zinc–copper cell is 1,10 V. Which change will INCREASE the emf?
choices: using larger zinc and copper electrodes
Larger electrodes lower the internal resistance: more current, same emf.
using a shorter salt bridge
A shorter bridge lowers the internal resistance: more current, same emf.
increasing the concentration of Cu²⁺ ions
More reactant (Cu²⁺) favours the forward reaction: the emf increases.
increasing the concentration of Zn²⁺ ions
More Zn²⁺ favours the reverse reaction: the emf decreases.
screens.why: C. emf changes only if the cell reaction is pushed forward or back. Electrode size and the salt bridge change only the current.

subject: Electrochemistry
